lede: A straight line has one gradient everywhere. A curve does not, which is what makes it good at describing something that speeds up or slows down: a car pulling away, a cup of tea cooling. The gradient of the tangent at a point is how fast the quantity is changing at that moment.
can: Draw a tangent at a stated point, with a ruler and long enough to read.
Find its gradient from two well-separated points on it.
Give the answer with the units the axes imply, and the right sign.

text: How fast is it changing right now?

md: Speed on a distance-time graph is the gradient, and on a straight line you read it once and you are done. Curves are the honest picture of most things: a kettle cools quickly at first and then slowly, so the gradient is different at every point. To get the rate at one moment you lay a ruler along the curve there and measure that line instead.

alt: The distance-time curve with both a dashed chord from t = 0 to t = 10 and a dashed tangent touching the curve at t = 6 seconds.
caption: A sledge: the chord gives the average speed of 2.5 m/s over 10 s, the tangent gives about 3 m/s at the instant t = 6 s.

prompt: What is the name of the straight line that touches a curve at one point and runs along it there?
explain: A tangent. Its gradient is the curve's gradient at that point, and drawing it is the single step that separates the top answers from the rest.

md:
Two different questions, two different lines.
**Average rate over an interval** — join the two ends with a straight **chord** and find its gradient. Total change divided by total time.

prompt: You are running out of time on a 2-mark 'estimate the rate' part. What is worth doing first?
options: Draw the tangent at the right point
Write down the value of the curve there
answer: Draw the tangent at the right point
explain: The first of the two marks is for a tangent drawn at the stated point. It costs one ruler line, and it is the mark most candidates never collect.

md:
**Rate at one instant** — draw the **tangent** at that point and find its gradient.
On a curve that bends, these give different answers, and the wording of the question tells you which one is wanted: 'over the first 4 minutes' means a chord, 'when $t = 4$' means a tangent.

prompt: A part asks for the rate of cooling **when** $t = 4$ minutes. Which line do you draw?
explain: 'When' names one moment. A chord would average the rate across four minutes, and the tea cools far faster at the start than at the end.

md: **Drawing the tangent well.** Mark the point of contact first. Lay the ruler so the line runs along the curve there — touching, not cutting — and draw it **long**, well past the point on both sides. Length matters because the gradient comes from two points on the line, and the further apart they are, the less a small reading slip costs you.

prompt: Why draw the tangent long rather than short?
options: So the two points you read from it are far apart and the gradient is more accurate
Because short tangents are not allowed
answer: So the two points you read from it are far apart and the gradient is more accurate
explain: A half-square error in reading a point barely matters over a run of eight units, and matters a great deal over a run of one.

title: Instantaneous rate of change
why: The tangent method from start to finish. Watch how the two points are chosen and how the axis scales turn into the units of the answer.

prompt: A tangent passes through $(3, 0)$ and $(9, 18)$ on a distance-time graph. What is its gradient?
explain: Rise $= 18 - 0 = 18$ and run $= 9 - 3 = 6$, so the gradient is $18 \div 6 = 3$. The units come next.

md: **The units come off the axes**: the unit going up, divided by the unit going across. Distance in metres against time in seconds gives m/s, which is a speed. Velocity in m/s against seconds gives m/s per second, written m/s², which is an acceleration. Temperature in °C against minutes gives °C per minute. Read the axis labels and the units write themselves.

prompt: A graph has area in m² up the side and time in weeks along the bottom. What are the units of the gradient?
explain: Vertical unit over horizontal unit. Turning it upside down is a common slip and it changes the meaning completely.

md: **The sign is information.** A tangent sloping downwards has a negative gradient, and that minus sign is the part of the answer that says *cooling*, *decaying*, *slowing down*. Writing $-5.5$ °C per minute and writing 'cooling at 5.5 °C per minute' both carry it. Writing $5.5$ on its own does not, and an examiner reads it as warming up.

alt: The same cooling curve with a dashed straight tangent drawn touching it at t = 4 minutes.
caption: A mug of tea cooling: the tangent at t = 4 minutes has gradient about -5.5 °C per minute.

prompt: The tangent to the cooling curve at $t = 4$ has gradient about $-5.5$. What does that mean?
options: The tea is cooling by about 5.5 °C every minute at that moment
The tea has cooled by 5.5 °C altogether
answer: The tea is cooling by about 5.5 °C every minute at that moment
explain: A gradient is a rate: how much the vertical quantity changes for each unit of the horizontal one. The minus sign makes it a fall rather than a rise.

title: Summer 2024 Paper 2 Q9
md: Candidates drew an exponential graph, read when the starting value had trebled, then had to estimate an instantaneous rate. The majority drew the graph — the value at $x = 0$ was the common loss — and a majority read it correctly. Only the stronger candidates thought to draw a tangent for the last part, and not all of those could work out its gradient. Two marks, and the first of them is for the tangent alone.

prompt: For a curve $A = 4(1.5)^t$, what is $A$ when $t = 0$?
explain: $1.5^0 = 1$, so $A = 4 \times 1 = 4$. Plotting that point at zero instead was the common loss in Summer 2024.

md: Counting squares only works when one square is one unit on **both** axes, and on these graphs it almost never is. If a small square is 0.2 seconds across and 1 metre up, a tangent rising 5 squares over 4 squares has risen 5 m in 0.8 s — a gradient of 6.25 m/s, not 1.25. Convert the squares into the units printed on the axes first, then divide. In Summer 2023 the examiners singled out an awkward grid scale as what made the whole question hard.

prompt: One small square is 0.2 s across and 1 m up. A tangent rises 4 squares over a run of 5 squares. What is its gradient, in m/s?
explain: Rise $= 4$ m, run $= 5 \times 0.2 = 1$ s, so the gradient is $4 \div 1 = 4$ m/s. Counting squares alone would have given $0.8$.

title: PhET: Calculus Grapher

task: Draw a curve that rises steeply and then flattens off. Move the point along it and watch the tangent turn. Find the place where the tangent is horizontal, and the places where it is steepest. Nothing here needs calculus: you are watching the gradient change from point to point, which is the whole idea of this statement.

title: A ten-second check
md: Ask whether the size makes sense in the story. A sledge a few seconds into a slope is not moving at 0.6 m/s; tea in a warm room does not cool at 50 °C a minute. A rate that is out by a factor of five is nearly always the scale trap, and a rate with the wrong sign is nearly always a dropped minus.

prompt: In the sim, what is true at the point where the tangent lies flat?
options: The rate of change is zero there
answer: The rate of change is zero there
explain: A horizontal tangent has gradient zero, so at that instant the quantity is momentarily not changing — the top of a hill or the bottom of a dip.

title: Sheet or memory?
md:
**On the Higher sheet:** nothing for this topic.
**Must be known:** rate at a point = gradient of the tangent there; average rate = gradient of the chord; gradient = rise ÷ run read from the axes; units = vertical unit ÷ horizontal unit; and a negative gradient means the quantity is falling.

prompt: Which of these is given on the Higher formula sheet?
explain: All of it is recall. The sheet stops at the cosine rule and ½ab sin C.

md:
Tell a chord from a tangent, and draw the tangent long.
Find its gradient from two well-separated points on it.
Read the units off the two axes.
Say what a negative gradient means in the story.

Two or three marks: draw a tangent at the named point, then work out its gradient with the axis scales. The first mark is the tangent itself, so draw it even when the reading defeats you. The last is the rate with its units. Stuck: draw the tangent and mark two points on it that sit on grid intersections.
